newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: INTERVIEW-MasterCard CEO says cash not dead yet.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-MasterCard CEO says cash not dead yet.

text.p: Cash and cheques are in no danger of losing their status as the preferred way to pay, but electronic payment systems should gain ground, the new president and chief executive officer of MasterCard International said on Wednesday.

"To predict the end of cash or the end of cheques is a leap of faith that certainly I am not willing to take at this time, but there are powerful motivators for getting rid of cash and cheque-based transactions," Robert Selander said in an interview with Reuters.
Expense is one big reason, he said, noting that studies have estimated the cost of administering cash and cheque-based transactions is as high as three or four percent of the gross domestic product.

"That's why I look at cash and cheques as the primary competition for electronic payments and I feel really good, because they're kind of benign. It's like shooting ducks in a barrel. No one is out there encouraging you to carry lots of cash," Selander said.
Selander, who assumed his posts this month, was in Seoul for MasterCard's annual Asia-Pacific meeting, which ends on Thursday.
More than 700 representatives of MasterCard and business partners, including banks, financial institutions and technology partners, attended Wednesday's session.

Electronic payments, which would include debit and credit card charges, account for no more than 20 percent of the consumer payments market in the United States, which is considered an advanced market, Selander said.
U.S. consumers are only just "beginning to begin" to use debit cards, he said.
Debit cards electronically transfer money from the consumer's bank account to the seller at the point of sale.

"The U.S. is a mature market because everybody in America has a credit card and virtually everybody who has a bank account has an ATM card or debit-capable card. But as a practical matter, people still use lots of cheques and lots of cash."
Selander said electronic payments would be unlikely to exceed 25 percent of the total U.S. consumer payment market in five or six years.

Reinforcing MasterCard's belief that the future of consumer payments is electronic, the company has signed a letter of intent to acquire 51 percent of Mondex International Ltd, developer of the Mondex electronic cash system.

The Mondex card stores "cash" on a chip and transfers it to another card. It differs from a debit card in that the Mondex transaction is conducted through a card-to-card transfer, while a debit card accesses a consumer bank account.

"If you believe in a cash replacement product, then the electronic cash alternative which doesn't require authorisation, settlement and clearance is the logical point where you would converge on over time. So I feel quite good about Mondex," he said.
Other Mondex shareholders include major financial banks and financial institutions in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong.
Selander said MasterCard would use Mondex as the chip-operating platform for its new Multi-application Operating System, or MULTOS, which he said would be an open system.
MasterCard has issued 400 million credit and debit cards worldwide. Its transaction volume exceeded $550 billion last year.
